stories.headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid affair with alleged Chinese spy; agrees to brief Congress

The resignation followed disclosures of two extramarital affairs.
The first affair was reported by the New York Times on Oct. 29.
The first affair involved businesswoman Alice Huang.

stories.headline: Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate seat, first Black senator from state since 19th century

claims.text: Democrat Scott Colom defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's U.S. Senate race.
The Associated Press race call was made Wednesday evening.
Colom won by approximately 5,000 votes.
Colom becomes the first Black senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction, nearly 150 years ago.

The Alaska Senate race remains undecided.

In 2023, Hyde-Smith blocked Colom's nomination by President Biden for a federal judgeship.

Hyde-Smith conceded the race Wednesday night.
Hyde-Smith stated she respects the decision of Mississippi voters.

facts: Sens. Ron Wyden (D-OR), incoming chair of the Senate Finance Committee, and Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD) sent a letter dated Wednesday to Children's Health Defense (CHD) launching an investigation into whether HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. lied to Congress.

The letter requests documents on Kennedy's 2019 Samoa trip, his 2024 presidential campaign, his Senate confirmation process, his September 2025 speech to CHD's convention, and all CHD communications with federal officials since Jan. 20, 2025.
CHD has been given a compliance deadline of Dec. 4.
During January 2025 confirmation hearings, Kennedy testified that his 2019 Samoa trip had 'nothing to do with vaccines.'

A January 2019 letter obtained by The Guardian and the Associated Press—via a Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press open-records lawsuit—shows Kennedy asked the Samoan prime minister to study MMR vaccine safety, using the words 'vaccine' or 'vaccination' eight times.
Samoa's 2019 measles outbreak, which began months after Kennedy's trip, caused 5,700 cases and 83 deaths, mostly children under five.
HHS has called allegations that Kennedy lied to Congress 'false' and 'outright defamatory,' saying the trip was 'unrelated to vaccines.'
Knowingly giving false testimony to Congress is a crime, though prosecutions are rare.
ladder.analysis:
The investigation targets the credibility of testimony Kennedy gave during his 2025 confirmation hearings, when he denied any vaccine-related purpose for a 2019 trip to Samoa that preceded one of the deadliest modern measles outbreaks. Documents obtained through litigation by press organizations appear to contradict that testimony, showing Kennedy directly raised MMR vaccine safety with Samoan officials before the trip. The probe, launched by the incoming Senate Finance Committee chair and a Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee member, uses a formal but non-subpoena letter to CHD, the anti-vaccine group Kennedy led until December 2024 and whose former staff now hold influential roles at HHS under him.

This action follows the Democratic Party regaining Senate control in the midterms, giving Wyden and allies subpoena power if CHD does not cooperate by the Dec. 4 deadline. The episode sits within a broader pattern of Democratic lawmakers signaling intent to scrutinize or seek accountability from Kennedy, while legal experts note that any Justice Department prosecution for false congressional testimony is unlikely under the current administration, making congressional hearings, subpoenas, or impeachment proceedings the more probable near-term mechanisms for accountability.
ladder.steelman: The dispute hinges on a factual contradiction—Kennedy's sworn claim that his Samoa trip had 'nothing to do with vaccines' versus a documented 2019 letter in which he raised MMR vaccine safety with Samoan officials—leaving the core question of intent and legal exposure unresolved pending CHD's document production and HHS's fuller response.
ladder.implications: If CHD misses the Dec. 4 deadline or provides incomplete records, Wyden has signaled he could escalate to formal subpoenas, intensifying the clash between the Democratic-controlled Senate and the Trump administration over Kennedy's tenure. The investigation could also feed into broader impeachment efforts already floated by some Democrats, even as experts caution that criminal prosecution for false testimony remains unlikely, making congressional oversight the primary avenue for accountability in the near term.

stories.headline: US envoys meet Putin in Moscow as Ukraine reports new Starshield disruptions
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters
body: US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday, a day after two days of US-mediated talks between Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi ended without a major breakthrough. The talks produced an agreement on a large prisoner swap, with the exact number still to be announced. Kushner described the meeting with Putin as "substantive and detailed," while Witkoff said a new round of trilateral negotiations had been set and suggested European representatives could be included for the first time.

Putin repeated his maximalist demands during the meeting, insisting that any foreign troops in Ukraine would be "absolutely unacceptable" and would be treated as legitimate targets, effectively resuming the war. He also proposed a five-day "humanitarian mission" to the contested frontline city of Kostyantynivka in eastern Ukraine, similar to a recent US-brokered evacuation in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky. Ukrainian presidential adviser Dmitry Lytvyn expressed skepticism, saying Russia used the Oleshky operation to bring in equipment and rotate troops under the guise of a humanitarian effort.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Thursday that Ukraine's military is facing new "systematic" restrictions to Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service. Zelensky said units have recorded significant disruptions and speed restrictions for several days, limiting Ukrainian drones to 161 kph (100 mph), and that a military investigation determined the restrictions were not random errors. "Unfortunately, this is helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine," he said. A similar disruption occurred in late October and lasted about a week before being resolved.

Zelensky spoke at a European Political Community summit in Dublin, where more than 40 European leaders gathered to discuss continental security and Ukraine. He said political changes, including Democrats taking over the US Congress in January and upcoming French elections, could create a "window of opportunity" for a peace deal, but insisted Ukraine will not surrender Russian-occupied territory. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said the US, Europe and Ukraine are "very much aligned" on security guarantees but need a ceasefire or peace deal first.

Fighting continues along the 1,200-kilometer front line. Russia launched 123 drones, 73 of them jet-powered, and missiles at Ukraine overnight, with hits recorded at 17 locations. Ukraine's military said it has struck seven Russian oil refineries in the last two weeks, including five of Russia's largest. A Russian serviceman was killed in a car explosion in St. Petersburg early Thursday; Russian media identified the victim as a colonel. The US envoys are expected to travel to Dublin to meet Zelensky after their Moscow talks.

stories.headline: Israeli airstrike on Gaza's Nasser Hospital kills six, including surgeon
body: An Israeli airstrike on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, southern Gaza, killed six people and wounded at least 28 others early Thursday, according to Gaza's Health Ministry. Among the dead was Dr. Rizq Abu Shaira, a general surgeon. The strike hit the hospital's surgical wing, causing extensive damage across multiple floors, with debris scattered over beds and equipment.

The hospital's director, Dr. Ahmed al-Fara, said two missiles struck the al-Yasin surgery building but only one exploded. He described the attack as a deliberate targeting of the health sector, noting that medical staff, patients, and companions were killed. Dr. Mohammed Qdeih, a surgeon wounded in the head, said he was trapped under rubble and recalled Dr. Abu Shaira as 'the kindest person in this department' and 'one of the best' surgeons.

The Israeli military said it carried out a 'precise strike' targeting Mohammed Abu Ismail, a commander of Hamas's Khan Younis Brigade, and other fighters who it alleged were using the hospital as a headquarters to plan attacks. Israel accused Hamas of storing weapons and operating command rooms inside the facility, a charge Hamas denied, calling the strike a 'war crime.' The hospital's director insisted no warning was given before the attack.

This was the seventh time Nasser Hospital has been struck during the war. Under international law, hospitals are protected, but can lose that status if used for military purposes. The World Health Organization said it has documented 1,056 attacks on healthcare in Gaza over the past three years, resulting in 1,010 deaths. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called for protection of health facilities, stating they 'must never be militarized or attacked.'

The airstrike comes despite a US-brokered ceasefire between Israel and Hamas that took effect in October 2025. Since then, more than 1,620 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's health ministry. The broader war began with the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on October 7, 2023, which killed about 1,200 people and saw 251 taken hostage. Since then, over 74,650 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says. The humanitarian situation remains dire, with heavy rains recently flooding tens of thousands of tents housing displaced families.

stories.headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after second affair, spying allegations
body: Jensen Huang, the 63-year-old co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, resigned on Thursday after revelations of a second extramarital affair, including one with a woman whom U.S. intelligence believes was spying for China. The announcement came after a board meeting late Wednesday, with Nvidia stating that Huang was stepping down immediately as president, CEO and board member. Chief financial officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor, ending Huang’s 33-year leadership of the AI chip giant.

The New York Times first reported that Huang had an affair with a senior Nvidia executive who reported directly to him. Both are married; Huang married his wife Lori in 1985. The second affair emerged just three days after Huang admitted a relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm that runs AI data centers across Southeast Asia and is a major Nvidia client. U.S. intelligence agencies concluded Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset passing information to Beijing; the intelligence behind that assessment remains classified. The U.S. government is also investigating whether Megaspeed secretly sent Nvidia chips to China, violating export curbs on high-end semiconductors. Megaspeed denies the allegations and has pledged to cooperate with investigators. Alice Huang has been barred from entering Singapore and Taiwan.

Nvidia’s market capitalization has fallen by well over $600 billion since the first affair emerged on Sunday, dropping to $4.2 trillion. Shares were down more than 9% in premarket trading Thursday, after falling 10% earlier in the week. The stock had hit all-time highs just a month ago as U.S. technology giants continued to announce billions in spending on AI infrastructure. Despite the turmoil, many analysts expect little impact on near-term sales due to high demand for Nvidia’s advanced chips. “While Jensen is the heart and lungs of the Nvidia story…the company and its leading-edge GPU technology will go on,” said Dan Ives, a tech analyst at Yorkville Ives.

Huang, known for his leather jackets and hands-on involvement in product decisions, had no formal succession plan, according to The Wall Street Journal. Bloomberg reported that Nvidia’s board is working with advisers to identify permanent successors. Potential candidates include Kress, other senior executives, and Huang’s children: daughter Madison, a senior director of product marketing, and son Spencer, who works in the firm’s robotics division. Longer-term possibilities floated by analysts include former Apple CEO Tim Cook and ex-Google CEO Eric Schmidt. Huang’s sudden exit is seen as disruptive to Nvidia’s relationships with AI hyperscalers, Taiwanese chip producer TSMC, and foreign governments, especially China, where he served as the company’s main lobbyist on chip export rules and persuaded President Donald Trump to ease some curbs last year.

The scandal has also intensified the U.S.-China AI rivalry. Beijing accused the U.S. on Thursday of using the spying claims as a pretext to impose a technological blockade on China. Chinese AI firms are reportedly trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centers outside China amid fears of further U.S. restrictions. The issue is expected to dominate talks next week between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC gathering in Shenzhen. Analysts see the biggest long-term risk in strategy and execution, as Huang was the leader who drove Nvidia’s bets on key technologies. However, some argue that Nvidia’s central role in the AI hardware buildout and its deep expertise in chip design and software make it less dependent on his day-to-day input.

stories.headline: Ukraine Strikes Russia's Largest Oil Refinery in Siberia, Completing Campaign Against Top Five Refineries
body: Ukraine confirmed on November 11 that its Special Operations Forces struck Russia's largest oil refinery, the Omsk Oil Refinery in Siberia, approximately 2,500 kilometers from the Ukrainian border. The attack, which involved deep-strike drones traveling up to 3,000 kilometers, set a new record for the farthest Ukrainian drone strike on a Russian oil refinery. The Omsk facility, owned by state energy giant Gazprom, processes over 21 million metric tons of crude oil annually and is responsible for one out of every six liters of Russian gasoline and diesel fuel.

According to Ukraine's General Staff, the facility has a refining depth of about 99%, one of the highest in Russia, and produces gasoline, diesel, aviation fuel, and petrochemical products that supply the Russian military. The attack caused a fire near the site, according to the independent Russian Telegram channel Astra, though the precise extent of damage was not immediately clear. Omsk Governor Vitaly Khotsenko reported that Ukrainian drones attacked the region for over eight hours, prompting air raid sirens, the closure of airspace, restrictions on mobile internet, and reports of blackouts in some districts. Khotsenko said emergency workers were dispatched to sites impacted by "falling drone debris" but did not specify which facilities were struck.

The Omsk strike was the latest in a broader Ukrainian campaign that, in less than two weeks, has hit all five of Russia's largest oil refineries. Since October 30, Ukrainian Defense Forces have also targeted the Kirishi, Ryazan, Nizhny Novgorod, and Yaroslavl refineries, as well as the smaller Novokuibyshevsk and Saratov refineries, according to the General Staff. The Kirishi refinery (KINEF) in the Leningrad region, with an annual capacity of about 20 million metric tons, was struck on November 9, damaging an atmospheric crude oil distillation unit, a primary oil-processing unit, and two cooling installations. The Saratov refinery, hit on November 7, suffered damage to its only primary crude oil distillation unit, two fuel hydrotreatment units, pipelines, and a 10,000-cubic-meter storage tank, forcing it to suspend operations.

Ukraine's General Staff stated that the strikes on primary oil refining units are intended to reduce fuel production for the Russian military and cut the revenues Moscow uses to finance its war. According to Reuters, citing two industry sources on November 10, Ukrainian drone strikes since late October have affected facilities representing nearly 30% of Russia's total refining capacity. President Volodymyr Zelensky has identified "long-range sanctions" as one of Ukraine's strongest forms of leverage against Russia, and the success of Ukraine's domestic long-range drone development has made targets deep in the Russian rear, such as the Omsk refinery, newly vulnerable to attack.

stories.headline: Spain approves housing reforms after nationwide strike over costs
body: The Spanish parliament passed housing measures on Thursday limiting evictions and real estate speculation, a day after a nationwide general strike over the country's housing crisis drew hundreds of thousands of protesters and sparked clashes in Barcelona. The interim lower house ratified the decrees in a 35–34 vote, but their duration depends on the outcome of a snap election scheduled for 29 November, in which the leading opposition Popular Party has said it will repeal the measures if it takes power.

The strike, Spain's first general strike in 14 years, was called by the country's main unions after parliament blocked earlier housing decrees. Some 120,000 people joined a demonstration in Madrid and more than 50,000 turned out in Barcelona, where masked men set fire to rubbish bins and smashed shop windows as police fired tear gas. Power usage in Spain fell by 7.5% during the early hours of Wednesday, according to data from operator Red Eléctrica, compared with a drop of more than 15% during the last general strike in 2012.

The housing crisis was triggered by widespread protests over affordable housing and rising living costs after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from a flat in Madrid where she had lived for seven decades. She died in hospital weeks later. Rental prices in the capital have risen sharply; the monthly cost of a 50 sq m apartment in Madrid averaged €1,170 in October, while Spain's average gross monthly salary is about €2,460, meaning rent consumes nearly half of gross pay, well above the 30% affordability threshold recommended by experts.

The first decree passed includes a measure extending protections against evictions for tenants deemed by social services to be in a precarious financial or social position, as long as regional authorities cannot offer them an alternative residence. Another measure aimed at reducing real estate speculation by stopping any company involved in the real estate market from buying properties for less than 70% of their value was rejected 34–35 after the centre-right Basque party voted with the right-wing bloc, arguing the measure could lead homeowners to withdraw properties from the market and drive prices higher.

Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called snap elections last month after parliament failed to approve his initial housing reform plan. He has encouraged workers to strike, writing on social media: 'Your eight-hour day. Your pension. Your public healthcare… These were collective conquests.' The conservative People's Party, which leads in polls, accused the government of weaponising the strike for electoral gain. PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo called the general strike 'nonsense' and the unions 'mafia' and 'trash'. Party spokesman Miguel Tellado accused the government of exploiting the strike to warn voters against allowing a right-wing government to be formed. Sánchez told Spanish TV: 'What is nonsense is to question the rights of workers to strike.'

stories.headline: Fed officials signal more rate hikes after hot CPI data
stories.byline: Financial & Markets desk · anchored on Reuters
body: Several Federal Reserve officials on Tuesday signaled that the central bank will need to raise interest rates further after a hotter-than-expected inflation report, though they differed on how quickly to move. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee called the latest consumer price index data "borderline disturbing" and said "we're going to have to deal with" the inflation issue. The October CPI rose 0.4% on a seasonally adjusted basis, the third straight month of outsized price increases and above economists' forecasts.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller said in London that a hot inflation reading could push him toward advocating for a half-percentage-point rate increase in December, an outsized move compared with the typical quarter-point hike. He specifically said such a hike should be on the table if core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy costs, came in "around 0.3" — which it did. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said she sees a need for two additional quarter-point increases and that "it may be possible to move more rapidly this winter." Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson took a more cautious view, saying "further gradual tightening seems appropriate."

The Federal Open Market Committee raised rates by a quarter point in September, to a range of 3.75%-4%, and held them steady in October. Waller, Logan and Paulson are voting members of the FOMC this year and will cast votes at the December meeting. Goolsbee will be a voting member next year. Goolsbee did not specify whether he favors a rate hike in December, saying he is "not a fan of being very specific and tying our hands." He noted that persistently high services inflation and the failure of tariff-driven price pressures to fade are key concerns.

Following the inflation data and officials' remarks, fed funds futures now unanimously expect a rate hike at the December meeting, according to CME's FedWatch tool. The odds of a half-point hike stand at 15%, while the probability of rates reaching 4.25%-4.5% by the January meeting — equivalent to either a single half-point rise or two quarter-point hikes — is 60%. There is a 10% chance of rates hitting 4.5%-4.75% by then. The debate over the pace of tightening reflects a broader question of how aggressive the Fed must be to return inflation to its 2% target after nearly six years of overshooting.

stories.headline: Stephen Curry out at least two weeks with oblique abdominal tear
body: Golden State Warriors star Stephen Curry has been diagnosed with an oblique abdominal tear and will be reevaluated in two weeks, the team announced Thursday. The injury occurred during the first quarter of Wednesday night's loss to the Houston Rockets, when Curry became tangled with Rockets forward Alperen Sengun. Video showed Sengun grabbing and twisting Curry's arm, after which Curry grabbed his side. He hit his lone 3-pointer of the game moments later, again grabbing at his side, and exited at the next dead ball, not returning. Warriors coach Steve Kerr said after the game that concern about the injury was "high" and that Curry told him he had "never done it before."

An MRI on Thursday confirmed the oblique abdominal tear. While two weeks is the best-case scenario for reevaluation, the timeline does not include any ramp-up process Curry would need before returning to the floor, meaning his absence could extend beyond that period. The severity of the tear is unclear; oblique strains—essentially minor tears—have sidelined NBA players for varying lengths in recent seasons, from Jose Alvarado's 10 days to Tari Eason's 37 days. More severe tears, such as those suffered by Orlando Magic's Paolo Banchero and Franz Wagner two years ago, resulted in absences of 10 weeks and more than a month, respectively.

Curry had been off to a scorching start to the season, averaging 30.1 points per game on 50.3/45.7/98.7 shooting splits as the Warriors won eight straight games for the first time since their 2022 championship season. The team entered Thursday at 8-4 with a top-three offense, but that margin is thin: Golden State is already without Jimmy Butler, Kristaps Porziņģis, Brandon Williams, and Gary Payton II, and wing Will Richard is playing through a ligament tear in his thumb. The Warriors now face their most difficult stretch of the season, beginning with a visit to the San Antonio Spurs on Friday followed by a back-to-back against the Dallas Mavericks and New Orleans Pelicans.

Curry is the latest NBA star to face an extended injury absence early in the 2026-27 season, joining a list that includes Jalen Williams, Chet Holmgren, Anthony Edwards, Tyrese Haliburton, Kawhi Leonard, Paolo Banchero, Jalen Duren, and Kon Knueppel. Any extended absence for Curry would be a brutal blow for the Warriors, who have little margin for additional injuries on an aging roster and are not equipped to cover for his absence.

stories.headline: Misiorowski and Schlittler Unanimously Win Cy Young Awards
body: Milwaukee Brewers’ Jacob Misiorowski and New York Yankees’ Cam Schlittler were named unanimous Cy Young Award winners for the 2026 MLB season on Wednesday, each receiving all 30 first-place votes from the Baseball Writers’ Association of America. Misiorowski, who led the Brewers to their first World Series title, posted a league-best 1.80 ERA among starters with 252 strikeouts in 30 starts, becoming the first pitcher since Randy Johnson in 2001 to win both the Cy Young and a World Series in the same season. Schlittler, in his first full season with the Yankees, recorded an AL-best 1.95 ERA with 239 strikeouts across 33 starts, allowing one run or fewer in 21 of those outings — a Yankees record.

Schlittler, 25, is the Yankees’ youngest Cy Young winner and the team’s first since Gerrit Cole in 2023. He beat finalists Dylan Cease of the Toronto Blue Jays and Parker Messick of the Cleveland Guardians. A seventh-round draft pick out of Northeastern University in 2022, Schlittler transformed from a pitcher whose fastball hovered in the low 90s to one who regularly touches 100 mph, throwing a four-seamer (averaging 98 mph), a sinker (97.8 mph) and a cutter (94.6 mph). He threw fastballs 89.2 percent of the time, the highest rate of any starter. Yankees manager Aaron Boone called him "the best pitcher in the league, hands down," while teammate Cole noted, "He gets an idea of how to dominate, and he dominates."

Misiorowski, 24, became the fourth Brewers pitcher to win the Cy Young, following Corbin Burnes (2021), Pete Vuckovich (1982) and Rollie Fingers (1981). He averaged 100.6 mph on his fastballs and threw more than 1,000 pitches at 100 mph or faster during the season. His fastball against the Chicago Cubs’ Pete Crow-Armstrong in June clocked at 105.5 mph, the fastest pitch ever thrown by a starter in the Statcast era. Misiorowski also led all pitchers with a 6.6 fWAR and a 0.80 WHIP. Phillies left-hander Cristopher Sanchez finished second in NL voting, with Braves veteran Chris Sale third.

Schlittler’s season included a notable snub when Toronto manager John Schneider picked Cease over him to start the All-Star Game, despite Schlittler leading Cease in ERA, WAR and games started at the time. Schlittler opted not to pitch in the game, instead resting as he accumulated a career-high 193 2/3 innings. He also continued a feud with fans of his hometown Boston Red Sox, whom he dominated in Game 1 of the AL Wild Card Series, throwing 117 pitches in a victory. The Yankees sometimes show Schlittler clips of people dissing him as motivation.

It is only the third time in MLB history that both Cy Young winners were unanimous picks, following 2022 (Justin Verlander, Sandy Alcantara) and 1968 (Denny McLain, Bob Gibson). San Diego Padres closer Mason Miller and Blue Jays closer Louis Varland won the inaugural Reliever of the Year awards for their respective leagues. Both Misiorowski and Schlittler have bright futures, with Misiorowski already holding a World Series ring and Schlittler established as the Yankees’ ace in a rotation that also features Cole, Carlos Rodon and Max Fried.

stories.headline: MLB Prepares for Possibility of MLBPA Disclaimer of Interest During Lockout
body: Major League Baseball is preparing for the possibility that the Major League Baseball Players Association (MLBPA) could file a disclaimer of interest during the upcoming lockout, according to a report from The Wall Street Journal. The current collective bargaining agreement (CBA) expires on December 1, and with no new deal expected by then, MLB will immediately implement a lockout, freezing all offseason activity. The 2021-22 lockout lasted 99 days, and the upcoming work stoppage is widely expected to be equally or more contentious.

A disclaimer of interest would mean the MLBPA temporarily steps down as the official union and sole bargaining unit for players, instead operating as a trade association. This would end collective bargaining negotiations without an agreement, and players would forfeit their protections under labor law but would be permitted to file their own antitrust lawsuits, likely as a class action, against MLB. One academic described the move to the Journal as 'the nuclear option,' as it would end any hope of reaching a negotiated agreement through the collective bargaining process.

The MLBPA has never disclaimed in prior negotiations, partly due to MLB's century-old antitrust exemption. However, the Curt Flood Act of 1998 opens the door for such action. The sides have managed to reach agreements in every subsequent negotiation without decertification, including in 2022, the first negotiation involving MLBPA executive director Bruce Meyer as the union's lead negotiator. Players associations in other leagues, such as the NFLPA and NBPA, have used this tactic during previous lockouts. The NFLPA disclaimed in the early 1990s, leading to a class-action suit that resulted in a jury finding the NFL in violation of antitrust laws and awarding players $543,000 in compensatory damages, tripled to $1.63 million under federal antitrust law. The NFLPA later petitioned the National Labor Relations Board for recertification to resume collective bargaining.

MLB has conditioned all its offers on a salary cap, which the union has repeatedly and firmly opposed. The parties have traded core economic proposals in recent months but remain far apart, with every MLB proposal conditioned on a cap and every union proposal conditioned on the absence of one. If the MLBPA were to disclaim, it would likely file an antitrust lawsuit in a different federal circuit than the one that ruled against the NFLPA in 2011, hoping for a different appellate outcome. MLB might argue that the disclaimer is a sham designed to undermine the negotiating process, and could raise claims of unfair labor practices under the National Labor Relations Act.

All parties would prefer a negotiated CBA over litigation. If the union goes this route, it likely would not happen until deep into the lockout. The possibility underscores the deep divide between the sides as the Dec. 1 deadline approaches.

stories.headline: Measles cases and costs surge as U.S. nears loss of elimination status
body: The United States is on the verge of losing its measles elimination status this week, as a committee of the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a regional World Health Organization body, meets for four days starting today to decide the matter. Cases have soared in recent years, with more than 5,000 reported nationally as of November 7 and at least eight deaths this year. In January, then-CDC official Ralph Abraham described the potential loss as 'the cost of doing business,' according to STAT.

Indiana has been particularly hard hit, with 145 confirmed cases in 2026. Knox County, Indiana, declared a public health emergency even though no cases have been confirmed there, in an effort to raise awareness and prevent outbreaks. One case has been reported in neighboring Daviess County. Knox County Health Officer Alan Stewart, M.D., said the best protection is vaccination, noting that 97 percent of Indiana cases have been in unvaccinated individuals. The emergency declaration allows the county to lower the vaccination age for children to 9 months, or as early as 6 months with a doctor's note.

In Ohio, Geauga Public Health confirmed a measles case on Wednesday, with exposure at seven locations in Geauga and Lake counties, including Berkshire Middle School, Kent State University's Geauga Campus, a restaurant, a choir concert, a sporting goods store, a steakhouse, and an urgent care center. The infected person was unvaccinated, according to Heather DiCioccio, director of nursing for the Lake County General Health District and Geauga Public Health. Officials are working to identify contacts, but the number of potentially exposed people is not yet known. Symptoms typically appear 7 to 21 days after exposure, meaning they could emerge through November 28.

Measles is extremely contagious, spreading through coughing and sneezing, and nine out of 10 unprotected people exposed will become ill. Health officials urge anyone who may have been exposed and is not immunized to contact their health care provider and monitor for symptoms, calling ahead before visiting a medical office. The Knox County Health Department emphasized that the measles vaccine is a safe, live attenuated virus. The U.S. elimination status decision from the PAHO committee is expected by the end of this week's meeting.

stories.headline: FDA shelves fast-track drug review voucher program launched under Trump
stories.byline: Health & Science desk · anchored on Reuters
body: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has shelved the fast-track drug review initiative launched during the Trump administration by former Commissioner Marty Makary, according to Reuters. The Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher program, launched in June 2025, aimed to slash drug review timelines to just one to two months for therapies addressing national priorities, such as urgent unmet health needs.

Critics pointed to possible preferential treatment for companies meeting demands of President Trump, such as offering drugs at lower prices. No new drugs have gotten a voucher since Makary’s departure, and a key component of the program — an executive council of political appointees that oversaw drug reviews and had a central role in speeding approvals — has gone dormant.

Separately, the U.S. Senate health committee has scheduled a pivotal vote for next week on the nomination of Heidi Overton to serve as FDA commissioner, despite lingering doubts from Republicans on the panel, STAT reported. The vote is set for Nov. 18 and, if it passes, her nomination would then go to the full Senate, where Republicans are racing to confirm nominees before Democrats take power in January.

Even as he scheduled the vote, committee Chair Bill Cassidy (R-La.) remained undecided on Overton, he wrote in a post on X. It would take just one Republican on the committee to sink her nomination, assuming all Democrats vote against her.

stories.headline: American Cancer Society revises guidelines, urges routine PSA screening for prostate cancer
body: The American Cancer Society released a major update to its prostate cancer screening guidelines on Thursday, recommending that men at average risk of the disease undergo routine PSA blood testing every two years starting at age 50. The new guidelines mark a significant shift from the previous 2010 recommendations, which left testing for average-risk men to their discretion after consulting a physician. For men in high-risk groups—specifically Black men and those with a strong family history of prostate cancer—the ACS now urges annual PSA screening beginning at age 45. The guideline authors said they hope increased surveillance will reduce the number of Black patients presenting with advanced-stage cancers, as this demographic is disproportionately represented in prostate cancer mortality.

The changes reflect recent findings that PSA screening reduced disease-specific mortality for certain men, bringing the biomarker back into specialists' favor after it had fallen out of routine use. PSA testing had been dropped from the ACS guidelines in 2010 due to its lack of specificity, which led to many men undergoing unnecessary follow-up procedures for cancers that were either absent or very slow-growing. The new guidelines also clarify the threshold for elevated PSA: a level of 3.0 nanograms per milliliter or higher for men aged 45 to 69, rather than the common but outdated cutoff of 4.0 ng/mL. “Most PSA blood tests in the United States, when they’re reported, say under 4.0 [ng/ml] is normal, but it really should be under 3,” said James Eastham, chief of urology at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. “I think [the update] will hopefully help primary care physicians refer folks a little bit earlier.”

To limit overdiagnosis and overtreatment, the guidelines now recommend that an elevated PSA result be confirmed with a second reading, followed by an MRI scan and/or testing for other prostate cancer biomarkers before proceeding to biopsy. “We just wanted to give a little bit of flexibility for folks who cannot easily obtain an MRI,” said William Dahut, chief scientific officer at the ACS and a contributing author of the guidelines, though he noted that an MRI would still be recommended prior to biopsy if a biomarker test came back abnormal. The guidelines do not endorse one biomarker over another; Dahut said ACS researchers plan to study which biomarkers may be more effective in predicting aggressive cancer. Eastham praised the approach: “There have been many men undergoing unnecessary biopsies, and many low risk cancers that were subsequently overtreated. … By recommending some steps between an elevated PSA and a biopsy, the new recommendations reflect the evidence that while being a good biomarker, PSA alone would identify too many men as biopsy candidates.”

The guidelines also address screening after age 70, stating that the decision to continue should be individualized because the balance of benefit and harm becomes less clear. Screening should be stopped after age 80 or in men not expected to live another 10 years. The ACS emphasized the importance of active surveillance for men with slow-growing cancer: “If you screen more men, you’re going to find more men with early-stage disease, and we need to be strong in our position that that does not mean that you need to rush for therapies or that you need to have therapies at all.”

Reaction from patient advocates was positive. Eddie Baynes, a 56-year-old prostate cancer survivor and Black man, said the new guidelines “hit the nail on the head.” He began getting regular PSA tests at age 52 after a fraternity screening event, which led to a cancer diagnosis and prostatectomy. “Part of my advocacy is getting tested more frequently. So now, just to have that announcement coming from the American Cancer Society, it just makes what I’ve been urging individuals to do for a while stronger,” he said. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, a federally appointed panel whose recommendations determine which preventive services insurers must cover, has not yet changed its own guidelines and continues to recommend against routine population-wide PSA screening, instead suggesting individualized decision-making. However, the task force has announced an upcoming update.

stories.headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid affair scandal and FBI probe into alleged Chinese spy ties
body: Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has resigned, the company announced Thursday, following revelations that he had two extramarital affairs — one with a woman U.S. authorities believe was a Chinese spy and another with a senior Nvidia executive. The 63-year-old co-founder, who led the chipmaker to become the linchpin of the global AI boom, will be replaced by chief financial officer Colette Kress on an interim basis. Nvidia shares fell more than 10 percent in pre-market trading after the announcement, a decline that would wipe off more than $400 billion in market capitalization.

The scandal erupted after reports that Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Megaspeed, a Southeast Asian buyer of Nvidia chips that U.S. authorities suspect of diverting advanced semiconductors to China in violation of export controls. The Financial Times reported that Alice Huang has surfaced in Beijing and is barred from Singapore for giving police inaccurate information. A second affair, with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, was reported Wednesday by The New York Times; CNBC said rumors of that relationship had circulated for years. The board met to consider Huang's ouster, and his resignation followed swiftly.

Megaspeed, Nvidia's largest Southeast Asian customer, has drawn intense scrutiny. The Straits Times visited its Singapore office and found no signs of activity; another tenant said it was always dark. The company's sole director, Tan Yong Pong, appears to have vanished. Short seller Culper Research alleged that over 20 percent of Nvidia's fiscal 2026 compute revenue was driven by China through illegal GPU diversion and Southeast Asian intermediaries. Nvidia reportedly intervened in a 2025 Commerce Department investigation of Megaspeed, halting the inquiry. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has become a fall guy, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronting him and more than half a dozen Republicans demanding answers.

The scandal extends beyond Megaspeed. Super Micro, a partner run by Huang's friend Charles Liang, is entangled in a separate case: three executives allegedly defrauded the U.S. by using a front company to buy $2.5 billion of Nvidia chips for Alibaba. Another firm, New Matrix, is an approved Nvidia buyer with ties to blacklisted Chinese military contractors. Huang had insisted Nvidia saw no evidence of chip diversion, but analysts say the board's decision to cut him loose suggests more allegations may emerge. Huang had no succession plan and was the only CEO Nvidia had ever known, with 60 direct reports.

The political stakes are high. President Donald Trump was informed about Huang's alleged spy girlfriend in 2025 and apparently took no action; Nvidia has reportedly donated $25 million to Trump's planned ballroom. Senator Elizabeth Warren, set to chair the Senate Banking Committee in January, has signaled interest in the matter. Democrats will control both chambers of Congress. If Huang knew chips were being diverted and facilitated sales, he could face criminal charges including bribery, espionage, and smuggling. Elon Musk posted on X that hiring Huang would be an honor, but the broader question remains how high the scheme reached and what else was an open secret at Nvidia.
